outcome: A preprint posted 21 March 2024 on Preprints.org proves the Feit–Thompson conjecture holds when p and q are twin primes (p = q+2), a genuine restriction of the general statement; it remains an unreviewed preprint with no evidence of subsequent journal publication, expert digestion, or independent citation, and no other case, bound, or resolution of the general conjecture was found in the window.
summary: The triage flagged a preprint (doi:10.20944/preprints202403.1214.v1), titled 'The Feit-Thompson Conjecture: An Example for Mathematical Research Based on Contradictory Sources,' posted to Preprints.org on 21 March 2024 (within the window). I could not fetch the PDF directly (preprints.org and researchgate.net both returned HTTP 403 to automated fetchers), so I relied on search-engine-rendered abstracts and secondary summaries of the abstract/content from Google's indexing of both the preprints.org page and the ResearchGate mirror, which agree closely on wording: the paper's stated result is a proof that p^(q-1)/(p-1) does not divide q^(p-1)/(q-1) when p and q are twin primes (p=q+2), i.e. the conjecture holds on the twin-prime sub-case. Twin primes are a restriction of 'all distinct primes p, q,' so this is a genuine case of the stated problem (removes territory from it), not a variant — it satisfies §3.1's test directly, confirming the conjecture on that slice (resolution_direction: confirmed). Nothing in any secondary summary of the abstract or the paper's declared dual purpose (the second purpose being methodological, about navigating contradictory web sources on the topic) mentions any AI system, so ai_role is 'none' with no basis_quote — I did not manage to read the full text due to the 403s, which is the main gap in this record (see incomplete). I found no evidence of subsequent peer-reviewed publication, journal acceptance, or citations of this preprint by other researchers; it appears to remain a single unreviewed preprint two and a half years after posting, which pushes toward classifying this as more provisional than a fully 'resolved' case. However §6.1 defines 'resolved' as requiring digestion, journal acceptance, or a directly checkable-by-hand argument for problems in general, and reserves 'claimed' primarily for cases lacking human verification of any kind; a self-contained elementary number-theory divisibility argument of this kind is normally checkable by a competent reader, and the paper explicitly frames itself as a proof, not merely an announcement or machine output. Given I could not personally verify the proof's correctness (I don't have the full text) and there is no sign any third party has, I classify this conservatively as 'partial' (a case of the problem addressed) with lower confidence that it would upgrade to 'resolved' on full inspection. I separately confirmed via the live Wikipedia article and independent search that the general Feit-Thompson conjecture remains open, that no counterexample to it has been found (the known 1971 Stephens counterexample applies only to the strictly stronger 'always coprime' variant, and predates the window in any case), that prior known cases are q=2 (Stephens 1971) and q=3 (Le 2012), both pre-dating the window, and that no q=5, q=7, or other new case, nor any AI-related claim, disproof, or bound, appears anywhere in the 2024–2026 literature I could locate.
competing_reading: If the preprint were read in full and found to contain a rigorous, checkable elementary argument, and if independent researchers have quietly checked it without generating a citable trail I could find, the correct status could arguably be 'resolved' for the twin-prime case rather than 'partial' — the codes aren't mutually exclusive in spirit, but §6.1's own hierarchy suggests 'partial' fits a case-of-the-problem result regardless of verification depth, so this reading doesn't change my classification, only the confidence in it. A stricter reading could also treat this as 'claimed' rather than 'partial' on the grounds that an unreviewed preprint with no independent verification hasn't cleared even a low bar of scrutiny, but §6.1 defines 'claimed' by contrast with 'resolved' for preprints in general, while 'partial' is explicitly a scope category (a case settled) that can co-exist with 'claimed'-level evidentiary weakness; I judged scope (case vs. whole) as the primary axis per §3.1 and used the outcome/summary to carry the evidentiary caveat.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the full preprint text directly (blocked by 403 responses from both preprints.org and researchgate.net during this session) to check the proof's correctness and look for any acknowledgements section; and checking Google Scholar/Semantic Scholar for citations or a later journal version of this preprint to see if it has since been formally reviewed or superseded.

events.what: Preprint on Preprints.org claiming to prove the Feit–Thompson divisibility statement when p and q are twin primes (p = q+2)
events.credibility_reason: Author unidentified in the record; the paper's title and declared dual purpose are methodological ('research based on contradictory sources'); no journal version, citation or expert uptake found in 2.5 years; and the researcher never opened the text, so the claimed content rests only on search-engine snippets.

judgement.doubts: F16: the only event was never opened (preprints.org and ResearchGate returned 403); its scope, correctness and AI disclosure (no acknowledgements read) are inferred from indexed abstract snippets. The record also renders the expression as p^(q-1)/(p-1), apparently a transcription slip for (p^q-1)/(p-1). Codes are left as written; if the preprint were read, it may deserve not_credible (unknown author, methodological framing, no uptake) and the status would fall to open. The twin-prime restriction, if genuine, is a legitimate case of the bullet.
